WHAT WAS WRONG (reproduced first, on the real registerType + recordEntry path, before any code changed): the generated per-type view claims a flat column namespace. SQLite does NOT error on a duplicate column name in a CREATE VIEW; it keeps the first and renames the loser to <name>:1. With envelope columns projected first, a property named 'source' yielded columns ["source","source:1","source_state"], and the exact query ARCHITECTURE.md prescribes returned {"source":"self","id":"e1"} -- the ENVELOPE value under the property's name, with no error. A wrong answer that looks right, which is the class this product exists to prevent.

THE FIX. @ascend/core owns the vocabulary: ENVELOPE_PROPERTY_NAMES (the 16 columns a view projects, in projection order), STATE_COLUMN_SUFFIX, reservedPropertyName(raw), and a NEW 'errors' bucket on Canonicalized<T> beside renames/warnings. Errors are a different KIND, not a higher severity: a warning is a legal spec someone probably did not mean; an error is one no canonicalization can rescue. registerType throws ReservedPropertyNameError before writing anything; refreshTypeViews->assertProjectable refuses before any DDL, as the second line for a version row that reached the store without the registry. packages/store/src/sql.ts projects FROM core's list, so the reserved set and the projected set cannot drift apart.

TWO SHAPE DECISIONS WORTH THE RECORD. (1) The _state suffix rule is UNCONDITIONAL even though a collision needs two properties, because versions arrive one at a time: admitting error_state in v1 would leave a registered family that v2 could never extend with 'error'. (2) reservedPropertyName canonicalizes its own input, so no spelling (Source, gitSHA, Recorded At) gets around the rule. Deliberately NOT reserved, measured rather than assumed: ascend_version and schema_version are entries columns the view does not project, so they stay legal; and '_state' canonicalizes to 'state', which nothing claims -- the real case is 'error_state', never the literal '_state'.

THE REPORT'S OWN PREDICATE IS PARTLY REFUTED -- this is the headline result, not a footnote. The finding as filed proposed "reject `.` and `\"`", and its boundary list named "a lone `$`". Measured against a real SQLite json_extract: `$.a\"b` returns the value stored under key `a\"b` (also with a sibling key `ab` present), `$.a$b` returns the VALUE, `$.a]b` returns the key `a]b`. Refusing those is the SAME defect as passing `a.b` -- it reports a working name as broken and sends an author to rename a property for no reason. So `.` and `[` are the only characters that break anywhere; `\"` and NUL break only at the START.

The character set is MEASURED, not read off the JSON path grammar. Every Unicode code point U+0000-U+10FFFF probed in 4 positions (leading, middle, trailing, alone) against a real SQLite json_extract: 4,448,256 probes, EXACTLY 12 failures, from 4 characters (`.` anywhere, `[` anywhere, `\"` leading only, NUL leading only). Lone surrogates (U+D800-U+DFFF) are unsafe and measured separately because the sweep skips them: json_valid still returns 1 and a sibling property (`$.ok`) still reads, so it is a per-property defect, not a whole-row blast radius. The decisive reconciliation ran the shipped guard against SQLite's actual behaviour for 4,456,448 names across all of Unicode: 0 false negatives, 0 false positives.

Two facts keep the guard the right shape.
